questions.question:
"The image of literature that we seek to sustain is tyrannically centered on the author..."**

What is the grammatical function** of the clause "that we seek to sustain"?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The clause "**that we seek to sustain**" functions as an adjective because it describes or identifies the noun "image."
 
• A **relative clause** (also known as an adjective clause) is used to provide essential or additional information about a preceding noun (the antecedent).
 
• In this sentence, the relative pronoun "**that**" introduces the clause and refers directly back to the subject "image."
 
• Thus, the clause is a **relative clause modifying "image"**.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Relative clause modifying "image"**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"The **image** of literature **that we seek to sustain** is tyrannically centered on the author..."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Adverbial clause:** This functions as an adverb and typically modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb, usually beginning with conjunctions like because, although, or when.
 
• **Independent clause:** This is a group of words that contains a subject and a verb and can stand alone as a complete sentence. "That we seek to sustain" is a dependent clause and cannot stand alone.
 
• **Noun clause acting as object:** A noun clause functions as a noun within a sentence (e.g., "I believe that we can win"). In the given sentence, the clause is modifying a specific noun rather than acting as a subject or object itself.

questions.question: Which sentence contains a correct use of the **passive voice** from the passage?

options.text: "The Author creates the meaning of the text."
"The text is furnished with a final signified."

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Passive voice structure:** The subject of the sentence receives the action instead of performing it. The formula is: **Subject + form of 'to be' + Past Participle**.
 
• In the sentence *"The text is furnished with a final signified,"* the subject is **"The text."**
 
• The verb phrase **"is furnished"** consists of the auxiliary verb "is" (form of to be) and the past participle "furnished."
 
• The "text" is not performing the action of furnishing; it is the recipient of that action, which is the defining characteristic of the passive voice.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"The text is furnished with a final signified."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1:** "The Author creates the meaning of the text." – This is in the **active voice** because the subject (The Author) is performing the action (creates).
 
• **Option 2:** "Language speaks the Author's intentions." – This is in the **active voice** because the subject (Language) is performing the action (speaks).
 
• **Option 3:** "Writing begins when the Author speaks." – This contains two clauses, both in the **active voice** (Writing begins; Author speaks).

questions.question: What does the word "tyrannically" most closely mean in the phrase "tyrannically centred on the author"?

__
 
• The word **"tyrannically"** means in a manner that is oppressive, unjustly harsh, or autocratic; resembling a tyrant, using power in a cruel or arbitrary manner.

 
 
• **Example:** The dictator ruled tyrannically, suppressing any form of dissent.
 
 
 
• In the phrase "tyrannically centred on the author," "tyrannically" implies that the focus on the author is done in a manner that is absolute and possibly oppressive or harsh.
 
 
• **Example:** The company was tyrannically centered on the CEO, with no room for dissenting opinions.
 
 

Therefore, the meaning of "tyrannically" in the given context is: **in a cruel and absolute way.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Rarely and unpredictably** (कभी-कभी और अप्रत्याशित रूप से): Happening infrequently and not in a predictable manner.
 
 
• **Example:** The weather in that region changes rarely and unpredictably.

questions.question: According to Barthes, what happens when we remove the Author from our understanding of literature?

options.text: The text gains the freedom to mean different things.
The author's life becomes even more important.
Interpretation is limited to historical context.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**Option 2**'.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• ***A) The text loses all meaning.***

 
 
• This **cannot be inferred** from the passage. Barthes explicitly states that refusing the Author does not mean refusing meaning.
 
 
 
• ***B) The text gains the freedom to mean different things.***
 
 
• This **can be inferred** from the passage. Barthes argues that without the Author, the text becomes open to multiple interpretations, allowing meaning to be created by the reader.
 
 
 
• ***C) The author's life becomes even more important.***
 
 
• This **cannot be inferred**. In fact, Barthes critiques the focus on the author’s life and intentions as limiting the text.
 
 
 
• ***D) Interpretation is limited to historical context.***
 
 
• This **cannot be inferred**. Barthes emphasizes that meaning is not fixed or limited but is instead an infinite play of signifiers.
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2: The text gains the freedom to mean different things.**

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1**: Incorrect because Barthes insists meaning is not lost when the Author is removed.
 
• **Option 3**: Incorrect because Barthes critiques the centrality of the author’s life and intentions.
 
• **Option 4**: Incorrect because Barthes rejects limiting interpretation to historical context; meaning is created by readers.

questions.question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

He had never seen (1)/ such a masterpiece (2)/ until he (3)/ visits the gallery last spring. (4)
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **option 4**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The primary issue in the sentence is the incorrect verb tense used in **part 4**.
 
• The sentence begins with the **Past Perfect tense** ("had never seen") and refers to a specific past time frame ("**last spring**").
 
• The verb "**visits**" is in the Simple Present tense, which is inconsistent with the past context of the sentence.
 
• The correct verb should be in the **Simple Past tense** ("**visited**") to match the timeline.

Therefore, the correct answer is **4**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"He had never seen such a masterpiece until he **visited** the gallery last spring."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **(1) "He had never seen"** – This part correctly uses the Past Perfect tense to describe an event that happened before another point in the past.
 
• **(2) "such a masterpiece"** – This part is grammatically sound, using "such a" correctly before a singular countable noun.
 
• **(3) "until he"** – This is a correct conjunction used to show the point in time when the state changed.
 
• **(4) "visits the gallery last spring."** – This is incorrect because the present tense "visits" cannot be used with the past time marker "last spring."

questions.question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

The professor's explanation (1)/ was filled in clarity (2)/ yet managed to obfuscate (3)/ more than elucidate. (4)
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The primary error in the sentence is the use of the incorrect preposition "**in**" after the word "**filled**" in **part 2**.
 
• In English, the standard phrasal verb to indicate that something is full of a particular quality or substance is "**filled with**."
 
• "**Filled in**" is typically used in the context of completing a form or a hole (e.g., "fill in the blanks").
 
• To maintain grammatical accuracy, "**filled in clarity**" must be changed to "**filled with clarity**."

Therefore, the correct answer is **2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"The professor's explanation was **filled with clarity** yet managed to obfuscate more than elucidate."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **(1) "The professor's explanation"** – This is the subject of the sentence and is grammatically correct.
 
• **(3) "yet managed to obfuscate"** – "Yet" is a conjunction showing contrast, and "obfuscate" (meaning to make obscure or unclear) is used correctly as an infinitive.
 
• **(4) "more than elucidate."** – "Elucidate" means to make something clear; this part correctly completes the comparison started in part 3.
 
• **Note:** While the sentence contains a semantic paradox (an explanation filled with clarity shouldn't obfuscate), the specific grammatical error is the prepositional usage in part 2.

questions.question:

__
 
• **Passive to Active Conversion:** To convert a sentence, the object of the passive sentence (the agent) becomes the subject of the active sentence.
 
• The original sentence is in the **Present Perfect Tense** (passive voice: *have been + past participle*).
 
• In the active voice, the Present Perfect structure must be: **Subject + has/have + Past Participle**.
 
• **Step-by-step conversion:** 
 
 
• Identify the agent: "the director" (becomes the new subject).
 
• Identify the verb tense: "have been signed" (Present Perfect).
 
• Identify the recipient: "the documents" (becomes the new object).
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"The director has signed the documents."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1:** "The director has been signing the documents." – This is the **Present Perfect Continuous** tense, which implies an ongoing action.
 
• **Option 3:** "The director is signing the documents." – This is the **Present Continuous** tense, indicating the action is happening right now.
 
• **Option 4:** "The director signed the documents." – This is the **Simple Past** tense, which does not match the Present Perfect aspect of the original sentence.

"Have last week's reports been sent to the committee yet?" the supervisor asked.

questions.solution:

__
 
• **Direct Speech:** "Did you submit the reports meant to be finalized last week to the review committee?" the supervisor asked.
 
• **Key Conversions:**
 
 
• **"whether... had been submitted" becomes "Did you submit"**
 
 
• The indirect question starts with "whether," which indicates a Yes/No question in direct speech.
 
• The Past Perfect tense in the indirect speech (**had been submitted**) correctly reverts to the Simple Past tense (**Did you submit**) in direct speech. While there is a shift from passive to active voice to make the direct quote sound more natural, it is the most accurate option provided.
 
 
 
• **"reports that were supposed to be finalized" becomes "reports meant to be finalized"**
 
 
• The phrase "meant to be" is a synonymous and accurate equivalent for "supposed to be" in this context, maintaining the original meaning regarding the missed deadline.
 
 
 
• **Reporting Verb:**
 
 
• The reporting verb "asked" remains the same and is placed at the end of the sentence in the direct form.
 
 
 
 
 
• **Punctuation and Format:**
 
 
• The direct question is correctly enclosed in quotation marks.
 
• It begins with a capital letter and ends with a question mark inside the quotation marks.
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 1**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"“Did you submit the reports meant to be finalized last week to the review committee?” the supervisor asked."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
